summary: Extends the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol so a client can ask a PCE to avoid certain things when computing a route. These are constraints that the client sets as exclusions in MPLS and GMPLS networks.

eli5.summary: When asking for directions, you might say avoid that bridge. This note lets a client tell the route-planning server which places to keep out of the route.

questions: how to exclude routes in pcep
what is the pcep exclude route object
how to exclude nodes in pcep
subtitle: How a PCEP client tells a path computation server which nodes, links and risk groups the route must avoid.

tldr.problem: A client asking a Path Computation Element for a route may need to keep certain nodes, resources or Shared Risk Link Groups off the path, for example to compute a disjoint backup path.
tldr.mechanism: A new Exclude Route Object (XRO) lists the things to avoid, each marked mandatory or merely desired. A new Explicit Exclusion Route subobject (EXRS) inside the Include Route Object limits an exclusion to one hop between two named elements.
tldr.outcome: PCEP can now express the route exclusions that RFC 4657 required. A Path-Key extension keeps parts of a working path confidential during diverse path computation.

today: RFC 5521 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2009. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it in the metadata for this site.

sections.title: Why Exclude Parts of a Route
sections.content:
A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute a path. It may want to name abstract nodes, resources and Shared Risk Link Groups (SRLGs) that must be left out. The RFC gives two examples. A PCE computing a secondary (backup) path may need it to be node, link or SRLG disjoint from the primary (working) path. Or an operator may want a path to avoid nodes that will soon be out of service.

Generic requirements for this came from RFC 4657, and PCEP itself is defined in RFC 5440. This RFC adds the PCEP extensions. RSVP-TE signaling of exclusions between network nodes is separately covered by RFC 4874.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you want a route that skips certain places, like a road under repair, or a second route that shares nothing with the first so one accident cannot block both.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Exclusion
sections.content:
Following RFC 4874, the RFC describes two kinds of route exclusion:

  • The Exclude Route List: nodes or resources excluded from the whole path.
  • An Explicit Route Exclusion: nodes or resources excluded only between a specific pair of abstract nodes in an explicit path.

The first is carried by a new PCEP object, the Exclude Route Object (XRO). The second is carried by a new subobject of the existing Include Route Object (IRO), the Explicit Exclusion Route subobject (EXRS).
sections.eli5: You can say avoid this bridge for the whole trip, or only avoid this bridge on the stretch between two towns.

sections.title: The Exclude Route Object
sections.content:
The XRO is OPTIONAL and MAY appear in Path Computation Request (PCReq) and Path Computation Reply (PCRep) messages. It has Object-Class 17 and Object-Type 1. Its body has a 16-bit Reserved field (zero on transmission), a 16-bit Flags field and then subobjects. An XRO with no subobjects MUST NOT be sent and SHOULD be ignored on receipt.

One flag is defined, F (Fail): the PCC wants a new path for an existing TE LSP that has failed. Then the old path MUST be given in a Record Route Object (RRO) in the request, so the computation can avoid double booking bandwidth.

Each subobject starts with an X-bit: 0 means the resource MUST be excluded, 1 means it SHOULD be excluded but MAY be included subject to PCE policy and the lack of a viable path. Subobjects can name an IPv4 prefix, an IPv6 prefix, an unnumbered interface ID, an autonomous system number or an SRLG. An Attribute field says how to read the subobject: 0 as an interface, 1 as a node, 2 as an SRLG. The RFC notes that, as in other PCEP and RSVP-TE objects, 4-octet AS numbers are not supported.
sections.eli5: The request carries a list of places to avoid. Each one is marked either must avoid, or try to avoid if you can.

sections.title: How the PCC and PCE Handle an XRO
sections.content:
The PCC builds an XRO of everything it wants excluded, clearing or setting the X-bit and choosing the Attribute for each entry. If a PCE finds more than one XRO in a PCReq, it MUST use the first and ignore the rest. A PCE that does not recognize the XRO MUST return a PCErr with Error-Type Unknown Object. One that is unwilling or unable to process it MUST return a PCErr with Error-Type Not supported object.

When computing, the PCE MUST NOT include any resource whose X-bit is clear, and SHOULD NOT include one whose X-bit is set unless no alternate path meeting the other constraints exists.

A PCE MAY also place an XRO in a PCRep. With a NO-PATH object, it shows which elements of the original XRO prevented a path. Without NO-PATH, the PCC SHOULD apply it as in RFC 4874 and the PCC or a corresponding LSR SHOULD signal an RSVP-TE XRO so downstream routers apply the exclusions.
sections.eli5: The planner must obey the must-avoid items. For the try-to-avoid items it only breaks the rule if there is no other way, and it can say which items made the trip impossible.

sections.title: Explicit Route Exclusion in the IRO
sections.content:
The EXRS is a new subobject of the Include Route Object, with type 33. It holds one or more of the same subobjects an XRO can hold, but the exclusion applies only to the single hop between the previous and next elements in the IRO. An EXRS MUST NOT be sent empty, and an empty one received MUST be ignored. Its L bit MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

If a PCE does not support EXRS, it answers as for a malformed object. If it supports EXRS but meets an unknown subobject inside it, the X-bit decides: when clear, it MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type Unrecognized EXRS subobject, giving the subobject type as Error-Value. When set, it MAY send that error or MAY ignore the subobject as local policy.

A successful PCRep MUST carry an ERO, which MAY contain exclusions using the EXRS as in RFC 4874.
sections.eli5: This lets you say avoid the bridge, but only between town A and town B, while still allowing it elsewhere on the trip.

sections.title: Exclusions with Confidentiality
sections.content:
For inter-domain diverse paths, a working path is computed first and a backup that must be disjoint from it is computed next, for example with Backward Recursive Path Computation (BRPC, RFC 5441). When domains belong to different providers, the working path may be returned with Path-Key subobjects (RFC 5520) in place of its explicit route, to keep it confidential.

So a Path-Key subobject may appear in the XRO of the backup request, with the L bit ignored. A PCE that sees one for its own domain turns it into ordinary XRO subobjects for its local computation. If it belongs to a different PCE, the PCE sends a PCReq to the identified PCE to expand it. Subobjects obtained this way MUST NOT be shared with other PCEs.
sections.eli5: If a company will not show its roads to a rival, it hands over a sealed note instead. Only that company can open the note and say which roads to avoid.

sections.title: Registry Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned object class 17 to the XRO, with object-type 1, route exclusion. The XRO may carry subobject types 1 (IPv4 prefix), 2 (IPv6 prefix), 4 (unnumbered interface ID), 32 (autonomous system number), 34 (SRLG), 64 and 65 (Path-Key with 32-bit and 128-bit PCE ID). IRO subobject type 33 is the EXRS, and PCEP error type 11 is Unrecognized EXRS subobject. A new XRO Flag Field registry holds the 16 flag bits, with bit 15 as the F-bit; new bits need an IETF Consensus action.
sections.eli5: Each new piece got an official number in the public list, so every implementation agrees on which is which.

sections.title: Manageability and Security
sections.content:
Finer control of paths raises the risk if a PCEP message is intercepted, modified or spoofed: an attacker could steer the computed path or make computation impossible. The RFC therefore calls the security techniques of RFC 5440 more important. It also notes that exclusions let an operator route around vulnerable parts of the network.

On manageability, the PCEP MIB module MUST be extended to show the exclusion extensions. How desired exclusions are treated, and what happens with an unrecognized XRO or EXRS subobject whose X-bit is set, should be configurable and open to inspection.
sections.eli5: Because the avoid list steers the route, a trickster who changes it could send traffic the wrong way. Protecting the messages matters more now.
